quick: Schizophrenia: 2-5 mg twice daily, titrated; most respond to 15-20 mg/day. Non-psychotic anxiety: 1-2 mg twice daily (max 6 mg/day, max 12 weeks)
May be taken with or without food
Use only if clearly needed; neonates exposed in 3rd trimester risk extrapyramidal/withdrawal symptoms
Excreted in breast milk; decide to stop nursing or the drug
Use with caution; no specific adjustment defined
Extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, NMS, CBC, LFTs
summary: Trifluoperazine is a high-potency first-generation (typical) phenothiazine antipsychotic used to manage schizophrenia and, for short-term/limited use, non-psychotic anxiety. It blocks dopamine D2 receptors. It carries a boxed warning of increased mortality when used in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (an unapproved use) and can cause extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
indications: Short-term treatment of generalized non-psychotic anxiety (not first-line; max 6 mg/day for up to 12 weeks)

dosage.d: 2-5 mg twice daily initially; usual optimum 15-20 mg/day (some need 40 mg/day or more)
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose; optimum response usually within 2-3 weeks
Do not exceed 6 mg/day or 12 weeks (tardive dyskinesia risk)

dosage.d: 1 mg once or twice daily initially, titrate; usually no need to exceed 15 mg/day
dosage.n: Adjust to weight and symptom severity

dosage.d: Lower end of dosage range; increase gradually
dosage.n: More susceptible to hypotension and neuromuscular reactions

admin: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed
May be given twice daily owing to long duration of action; some patients maintained once daily
Increase dose more gradually in debilitated, emaciated, or elderly patients
Reduce gradually to a maintenance level once maximum response is achieved; avoid abrupt high-dose changes
Persons with known phenothiazine sensitivity should avoid direct skin contact with the drug
moa: Trifluoperazine is a piperazine phenothiazine that acts primarily by blocking postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic system, reducing psychotic symptoms. It also has antagonist activity at other receptors (alpha-adrenergic, histaminergic, muscarinic) accounting for its adverse-effect profile.

absolute: Comatose or greatly CNS-depressed states (e.g., due to CNS depressants)
Existing blood dyscrasias or bone marrow depression
relative: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (boxed warning - increased mortality; not approved)

preg: There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use only if clearly needed. Neonates exposed to antipsychotics during the third trimester are at risk for extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding difficulty) after delivery. If extrapyramidal symptoms occur in a pregnant patient, the drug should be stopped and not restarted.
lact: Phenothiazines are excreted in human breast milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the nursing infant, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or to discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is defined; use with caution as reduced clearance may increase exposure and adverse effects.
hepatic: Contraindicated in pre-existing liver damage. Cholestatic jaundice has occurred with phenothiazines; use with caution and monitor liver function.

major: Other CNS depressants and anesthetics/opioids (additive sedation and respiratory depression)
moderate: Anticholinergic drugs (additive anticholinergic effects, may reduce antipsychotic efficacy)
Propranolol (increased plasma levels of both drugs)
Anticonvulsants (lowered seizure threshold; may need dose adjustment)
minor: Antacids (may reduce phenothiazine absorption - separate dosing)
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive pregnancy tests; may alter blood counts and liver function tests; can affect PKU and urinary metabolite assays

serious: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperpyrexia, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability)
rare: Photosensitivity and skin/eye pigmentation with prolonged high-dose use
emergency: Severe acute dystonia compromising the airway

monitoring: Extrapyramidal symptoms and regular assessment for tardive dyskinesia
Signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, mental status change)
Complete blood count (especially if signs of infection)
Blood pressure (orthostatic hypotension), ECG/QT in at-risk patients
counsel: It may take 2-3 weeks to see the full benefit; do not stop suddenly without talking to your doctor
It can cause drowsiness and dizziness - avoid driving until you know how it affects you, and rise slowly to avoid fainting
Avoid alcohol; tell your doctor about uncontrolled movements of the face, tongue, or limbs
Seek urgent care for high fever with muscle stiffness and confusion, or for muscle spasms of the neck/throat or difficulty breathing
Use sun protection (photosensitivity) and report sore throat, fever, or yellowing of the skin/eyes
pk: Antipsychotic effect develops over days to weeks; sedation sooner
Plasma peak approximately 1.5 to 4 hours after an oral dose
Long; supports once- or twice-daily dosing
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from moisture and light; dispense in tight, light-resistant container
pearls: BOXED WARNING: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (not approved for this use)
High-potency phenothiazine - more extrapyramidal symptoms and less sedation/hypotension than low-potency agents like chlorpromazine
For non-psychotic anxiety, limit to <=6 mg/day and <=12 weeks to reduce risk of tardive dyskinesia
Watch for neuroleptic malignant syndrome - a medical emergency; stop the drug and provide supportive care
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule - do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose causes extrapyramidal/dystonic reactions, CNS depression (somnolence to coma), agitation, convulsions, ECG changes and arrhythmias, fever, hypotension, dry mouth, and ileus. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive: maintain the airway (dysphagia/respiratory difficulty may occur), avoid inducing emesis (risk of dystonic aspiration), early gastric lavage may help, treat extrapyramidal symptoms with anti-parkinsonism drugs or diphenhydramine, and manage hypotension with norepinephrine or phenylephrine (NOT epinephrine, which can paradoxically lower blood pressure). Phenothiazines are not effectively dialyzable.
